# Can the numerical tools be trusted? {#sec-trust}

## Motivation

Every later conclusion about learning assumes that the differentiable forward model reproduces the benchmark's data, that
its gradients are correct, that the score we optimise and report is the benchmark's own score, and that the model is not
simply a different physics from an independent simulator. A negative result from a faulty projector would say nothing
about the science, so these checks came first. The forward model in question maps the three material volume fractions in
each pixel to the transmitted fraction $T_k$ at each tube voltage $k$ through the polychromatic Beer-Lambert law
(@eq-beer), integrated along every ray of a fan-beam scan.

The evidence is of uneven strength, and it is worth saying so first. The comparison with the official generator and the
gradient check are each recorded in a single experiment summary that has not had an independent review. The comparison with
an independent simulator was reviewed once, and the review found an error (described below); the corrected result is
itself still awaiting review. The remaining checks are preliminary findings. None of these checks used real scanner data.

Two different forward models appear in this chapter and they should not be confused. The first is the **benchmark
pipeline** used for all learning experiments in this guide: a fan-beam projector with the benchmark's published spectra,
attenuation tables and geometry, for adipose, fibroglandular tissue and calcification. The second is the project's earlier,
more general model (water, calcium and iodine, with the project's own spectra and attenuation tables), which was compared
with an independent simulator. A check of one does not transfer to the other, because they use different spectra and
different material tables.

## What was verified

*Agreement with the official generator.* [Our projector and polychromatic forward model reproduce the official benchmark
generator's transmissions to float32 rounding on the starting-kit and dataset cases, with the largest error about 3.3 times
below the tolerance derived beforehand.]{#clm-0020 .claim} The comparison used the 10 starting-kit cases and 40 evenly
spaced dataset cases, both tube voltages, and it holds under the model the benchmark shares with us (its published spectra,
attenuation tables and geometry, unit incident intensity, no noise). The largest absolute difference in transmission was
$3.6\times10^{-7}$ and no ray exceeded the tolerance. The tolerance was derived from float32 error propagation before the
comparison, not tuned to the result. The official projector integrates over each pixel layer by layer; at reduced
resolution (64 and 128 pixels, one starting-kit case) it agreed with an exact chord-length integral to within
$4.3\times10^{-14}$ cm, so the official layered projector is, to rounding, the exact line integral. The comparison is
against the official generator's own forward model, so it shows that we implemented that model correctly, not that the
model is a faithful description of a scanner. The first attempt at this
comparison failed because of an error in our driver script (it looked for the starting-kit cases among the 1000 dataset
cases, where they are not present); it was recorded, fixed and rerun, and produced no physics result.

*Gradients.* [Automatic-differentiation gradients of the projection loss agree with central finite differences (median
relative error $9.4\times10^{-9}$ on a small geometry, $1.5\times10^{-7}$ on the full $512\times512$ geometry at sampled
entries).]{#clm-0021 .claim} These medians are for the loss on transmissions in double precision; the worst sampled entries
were off by about $10^{-6}$ (relative), and variants of the loss on $-\ln T$ gave medians between $6\times10^{-9}$ and
$2.3\times10^{-7}$. Gradients are finite and non-zero for all three materials, single- and double-precision
gradients agree to a relative $2\times10^{-7}$ in the Euclidean norm, and gradient descent from a valid but wrong starting
point on a tiny phantom reduced the loss by 99.8%. The check samples 60 entries on the small ($24\times24$-pixel) geometry
and 12 on the large one, and both use only 16 of the view positions, so it makes a gradient bug unlikely, not impossible.
The optimisation test generated its data with the same model it then inverted, so it is not a test of model mismatch. It verifies the differentiable
physics, not that minimising the loss recovers the right materials, which is the subject of @sec-labelfree.

*A property of the forward model that constrains the learning code.* [With unconstrained network outputs the polychromatic
forward model produces non-finite projection errors, because negative fractions give negative path lengths and the
exponential of a large positive attenuation overflows; every physics-trained network therefore needs a non-negative output
parameterisation.]{#clm-0090 .claim} This was found in the first supervised smoke test, which also missed its
pre-registered loss-reduction criterion because it was too short; both problems were fixed before the rerun that passed.

*The score and the acquisition conventions.* The benchmark's primary score is the mean over cases of the per-case
root-mean-square error of the volume fractions over the three materials and all $n_x n_y$ pixels (@eq-s1), with
$\hat f$ the estimate, $f$ the truth and $C$ the number of cases:

$$
s_1 \;=\; \frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\sqrt{\frac{1}{3\,n_x n_y}\sum_{m=1}^{3}\sum_{x,y}\bigl(\hat f_{c,m}(x,y)-f_{c,m}(x,y)\bigr)^2}.
$$ {#eq-s1}

[Our implementation of the benchmark's primary score reproduces the official starting-kit formula to $10^{-12}$ relative
tolerance on a random four-case test, including the kit's different array axis order.]{#clm-0091 .claim} The test used
$16\times16$ images and was a unit test, not a registered run; the official divisor on the real task is
$3\times512^2$ per case, and the records state that scores at reduced resolution are not comparable with published values. A
separate source-code reading checked the second, tie-breaking score as well, including a kit quirk that omits the last
region-of-interest position. [The kit applies kVp switching by interlacing: the 80 kVp measurement is carried by the even
views and the 50 kVp measurement by the odd views of a 512-view circular fan-beam scan, and our convention matches the kit's
source code; the kit's projector itself builds the full 512-view sinogram and the split is applied afterwards, so the stored
256-view arrays for each voltage are every other view, not contiguous angular sweeps.]{#clm-0092 .claim} Any
projection-domain code must therefore apply the parity split itself. This was verified by reading the kit source, not by a
numerical experiment.

*Agreement with an independent simulator (the earlier general model).* [With the reference simulator's own spectrum,
detector weights and attenuation, the earlier general-purpose model reproduces it to 0.47-1.05% (0.26-0.47% with
voxel-marched chords), a check of the adapter and geometry because the transport equation is shared; replacing the
spectrum with our own raises the mismatch to about 2.4-3.2%, the largest single term (synthetic disk phantoms, no scatter,
preliminary).]{#clm-0022 .claim} The percentages are relative root-mean-square differences in $-\ln T$ (the log attenuation
of the transmitted fraction $T$) on rays through the object, over three disk phantoms at 80 and 120 kVp. A point-binned
spectrum convention gives 2.1-2.7% and a half-bin shift of the bin edges 4-6%, so only "about 2-3% or more" is robust. The
spectrum term compares two different spectrum specifications (the reference simulator's tungsten-target spectra and our own, whose
filtration was not verified), ours being systematically softer, so it measures sensitivity to the spectrum specification
and is not an error of either. Changing the attenuation tables moved projections by only 0.1-0.2%, and the detector response
by at most 0.25% (the superseded earlier version of the finding said at most about 1%; the corrected finding is used here). [An earlier version of this comparison double-counted photons in a binning window at 80 kVp and reported
2.1-2.6%; an independent review caught the error and the corrected, larger number replaced it.]{#clm-0093 .claim} The corrected finding still needs its own review. The comparison was single-ray, one detector row, with no scatter
no photon counting and no reconstruction-domain comparison, and the reference simulator is itself a model, not the truth.

*Reproducibility across machines.* This check concerns the reference simulator, not our model. [The reference simulator, run
from one frozen source and configuration on the cluster, reproduced its own laptop result to a maximum absolute difference of
$9.66\times10^{-6}$ in $-\ln T$ and reconstructions to 0.0133 HU (not bit-identical; a patched build; one phantom, one tube
voltage, noise-free, CPU only).]{#clm-0023 .claim} It shows that the workflow for moving computations to the cluster does
not change results appreciably. Two earlier cluster attempts failed on a line-ending defect in the simulator's source
distribution, which is why the build was patched (the source archive was hash-verified; only the build scripts' line endings
were changed).

## The data and the split

[The 1000-case benchmark release was checksum-verified and split once, before any training, into 800 training, 100
validation and 100 test cases with no duplicate phantoms; all cases share a single support mask, so occupancy-based ideas
cannot be tested for generalisation to new supports on this dataset, and the test split has not been
used.]{#clm-0058 .claim} The ten starting-kit cases are not among the 1000, so they form a small out-of-sample check on the
same support. Duplicate detection is by exact byte hash, so near-duplicates are not excluded, and the release carries no
patient-level grouping because the phantoms are synthetic. The shared mask also means that "knowing where tissue is" is
knowing one fixed image, a point that matters for the occupancy-based network outputs in @sec-labelfree.

## How citable are the runs?

A computed result is only as useful as the code that produced it can be identified. The project records, for every run, whether
the working tree had uncommitted changes. [Early in the project the whole-tree "uncommitted changes" flag was found to
mark runs as not citable merely because the provenance system was writing its own log into the repository while the run
executed; there turn out to be two whole-tree flags, sampled at different moments, which legitimately disagree, and the project
therefore uses a third flag, restricted to source files, as the citability signal.]{#clm-0094 .claim}
The history is untidy and is told here as it happened. We first stated that the whole-tree flag is always true during a run;
a reviewer pointed to a run that recorded it false; that statement was first conceded and then restored when both records
turned out to be correct but sampled at different times. The supporting finding remains preliminary and rests on run records
without numerical metrics. [A later engineering decision widened the first, narrower definition of "source" (source code, tests and configurations
only) to one definition for citability (source code, tests, configurations, scripts, the project directories, the project
metadata file and the dependency lock file, with result directories counted as outputs), shared by the run metadata and the
pre-launch checks; a run with unknown source state is never citable.]{#clm-0095 .claim}
The learning runs examined for this guide (the reference supervised run, the baseline label-free run and the structured
label-free run) were recorded by the provenance system with a clear whole-tree flag at launch. This is a statement about the process, not
about correctness; it also does not mean that every run in the project is citable, and this guide does not audit every run.

## What this does and does not establish

[These checks establish that the numerical stack agrees with the benchmark generator and with itself; they say nothing about
real-scanner accuracy, noise, scatter or spectral error.]{#clm-0024 .claim} They make a bug in the projector an unlikely
explanation for the negative results that follow, and they do not show that conclusions about the benchmark carry over to
clinical data (@sec-open). One limitation is structural: the benchmark data were generated by the same model our
projector implements, so agreement is expected, and the checks cannot reveal how much a different, more realistic generator
would change the answers. The spectrum comparison above, made with the earlier general model, shows that such a difference
can be a few per cent in projections.
